opus-5.5.text:
Because what matters isn't how much money you have, it's what that money can buy. Cash feels safe because its nominal value doesn't bounce around, but that's an illusion. If you earn a low interest rate and then pay taxes on it, while inflation is running higher, your buying power is quietly going down year after year. You don't get a statement telling you that you've lost money, so most people don't notice, but over time it compounds in the wrong direction.

There's also a bigger, historical reason. I've studied the rise and fall of reserve currencies and major empires going back hundreds of years, and there's a pattern that repeats. Governments build up too much debt, more than they can realistically pay back. When that happens, they have a choice: they can squeeze people through painful austerity and defaults, or they can print money and devalue the currency. Almost always, they end up printing, because it's the least painful path politically. And when they do, the people holding the debt and the cash are the ones who pay for it. Over the long sweep of history, nearly every currency has either been badly devalued or has disappeared altogether.

So when you hold cash for the long term, you're really holding a claim on a government's promise at exactly the time when that promise may be getting weaker.

Now, I'm not saying cash is useless. It has a role for liquidity, for meeting your near-term needs, and for giving you the ability to act when there are opportunities. But it's a poor way to store wealth over the long term. You're better off owning a well-diversified mix of assets, across countries and asset classes, including some that do well when currencies are being devalued, like gold. The important thing is to think in terms of real returns, meaning what you have after inflation and taxes, because that's what determines your actual wealth.

r001.rationale: It says cash earns a low interest rate that is taxed while inflation is higher, reducing buying power.

r002.rationale: The response discusses inflation, currency devaluation, and diversification, but does not identify productivity growth as a source of investment returns.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, people think cash is safe because they look at its value in nominal terms and it doesn't go up and down. But that's the wrong way to think about it. What matters is your buying power, and cash loses buying power over time because of inflation. If you're holding cash and inflation is running at, say, three or four percent, and you're earning less than that, you're losing money every year. You just don't see it because the number in your account looks the same.

And it's not an accident. Governments and central banks, when they have a lot of debt, which they do now, they have a strong incentive to print money. That's how they deal with debt problems. They don't default in a visible way, they devalue the currency. So throughout history, if you look at it, cash has been the worst-performing asset class over long periods. It's taxed through inflation, quietly.

So what I say is, cash is trash as a long-term holding. It's useful for liquidity, for being able to move, for being able to buy when things are cheap. But as a store of wealth over ten, twenty, thirty years, it's a losing proposition. You want to own things that hold their value in real terms, that produce something or that have scarcity, and you want to be diversified across them. That's how you protect yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says inflation quietly taxes cash, but does not state that cash earnings may be taxable even when there is no after-inflation gain.

r002.rationale: The response recommends owning things that produce something, but does not identify productivity growth as a source of investment returns.

astra-6.text:
Because people confuse stability in the price of cash with stability in its purchasing power. A dollar is still a dollar next year, but what can it buy? If the interest you earn is less than inflation, you’re losing purchasing power, even though your account balance may be going up.

Now, cash has a purpose. You need it to meet your expenses, and it gives you flexibility when opportunities come along. But that’s different from saying it’s a good place to store wealth for decades.

What matters is your return after inflation and taxes. And rather than making one big bet on cash—or on anything else—you want a well-diversified portfolio that can do reasonably well in different economic environments.

r001.rationale: It mentions evaluating returns after inflation and taxes, but does not state that cash earnings may be taxable even when they produce no gain after inflation.

r002.rationale: It recommends diversification across economic environments but does not identify productivity growth as a source of investment returns.

sol-6.1.text:
Because people confuse a stable price with stable purchasing power. A dollar is still a dollar next year, but if prices have gone up, it buys you less. What matters is the return you earn after inflation and taxes. If that return is negative, your cash is steadily losing value, even though the number in your account looks safe.

Cash has a purpose. You need liquidity to meet your obligations, and having some gives you flexibility when opportunities arise. But holding cash for decades is different. For long-term wealth, you want a well-diversified portfolio of assets that can generate returns and preserve purchasing power. The question isn’t just, “Can I lose money?” It’s, “What will this money actually buy me in the future?”

r001.rationale: The response says to consider returns after inflation and taxes, but does not state that cash earnings can be taxed even when they produce no gain after inflation.

r002.rationale: The response mentions assets that can generate returns, but does not identify productivity growth as a source of investment returns.
